beats.headline: Is your date handling thread-unsafe?
beats.subline: Stop using java.util.Date. It's mutable, confusing, and leaks memory.
beats.narration: If you are still using java dot util dot Date, you are building on a landmine. It is mutable and thread-unsafe. Modern Java replaced it with the java dot time package.

beats.title: Legacy vs. Modern Time

top.label: Legacy (Date)
top.code:
Date d = new Date();
d.setYear(125); // Mutable!

bottom.label: Modern (Instant)
bottom.code:
Instant now = Instant.now();
Instant later = now.plusSeconds(60);

beats.narration: Legacy date objects are mutable, meaning any caller can change your timestamp. Modern Instant objects are immutable, making them safe to share across threads without locks.

beats.title: Machine vs. Human Time

steps.explanation: Use for DB timestamps and logs. It is an exact point on the UTC timeline.
No time zone. Perfect for birthdays or store hours.
Handles DST and historical zone rules automatically.

beats.narration: Use Instant for machine timestamps, LocalDate for calendar dates, and ZonedDateTime when you need to respect specific regional daylight saving rules.

beats.title: Duration vs. Period
beats.subtitle: Choosing the right interval type

nodes.label: Pitfall
nodes.detail: Period ignores DST; Duration tracks physical time

beats.narration: Don't mix these up. Duration tracks physical time for latencies, while Period tracks calendar time for billing cycles. Adding a day across a DST transition behaves differently for each.

beats.title: Part 1 Done
takeaways: Instant for UTC, LocalDate for calendar

beats.headline: Still using trim() for whitespace?
beats.subline: It is legacy code. Modern Java offers smarter, Unicode-aware alternatives.
beats.narration: If you are still using trim to clean strings, you are missing out. It only handles ASCII. Modern Java offers better tools for real-world text processing.

beats.title: Modern String Methods

steps.explanation: Unicode-aware whitespace removal. Better than trim().
Splits strings into a lazy stream of lines.

beats.narration: Strip is Unicode-aware, unlike trim. Repeat is a clean way to build separators, and lines lets you process multi-line input as a stream.

beats.title: Text Blocks (Java 15+)
beats.code:
String sql = """
    SELECT * FROM users
    WHERE id = ?
    """.formatted(userId);

steps.explanation: Multi-line strings without manual \n or + concatenation.
Clean interpolation for your text blocks.

beats.narration: Text blocks let you write SQL or JSON naturally. Use formatted to inject variables without breaking readability. It is the end of messy string concatenation.

beats.title: Locale-Aware Formatting
beats.narration: Always use Locale dot ROOT when formatting numbers for wire formats. The default locale might use commas, which will break your JSON parsers.

beats.title: Part 2 Done
takeaways: Text blocks for clean multi-line strings
Always use Locale.ROOT for wire formats

beats.headline: Stop writing 5 lines to create a List.
beats.subline: Java 9+ factories make collections concise, immutable, and safer.
beats.narration: Creating a list used to take multiple lines. Modern Java factories make this trivial, safer, and more memory-efficient.

beats.title: Concise Collection Factories

steps.explanation: Creates an immutable, fixed-size list instantly.
Clean map creation for small key-value pairs.

beats.narration: These factories are immutable, reject nulls, and are highly memory-optimized. They are the standard for small, read-only collections.

beats.title: Factory vs. Wrapper
beats.narration: Don't confuse these with the old unmodifiable wrappers. List dot of creates a new, truly immutable instance that does not depend on a mutable backing collection.

beats.title: Why Nulls Fail
beats.caption: Fail-fast design

lines.text: # Factories reject nulls to prevent bugs

beats.narration: These factories reject nulls immediately. This fail-fast behavior catches bugs at creation time rather than later when you try to use the collection.

beats.headline: Stop blocking threads for HTTP calls.
beats.subline: The Java 11 HttpClient supports HTTP/2, async, and streaming.
beats.narration: Old HTTP connections are blocking and slow. The modern HttpClient supports HTTP/2, asynchronous requests, and streaming, all built into the JDK.

beats.title: Building the Client

steps.explanation: Create once, reuse everywhere. It manages connection pools.
Always set a connect timeout to avoid hanging.
Off by default. Enable for standard web behavior.

beats.narration: Configure the client once and reuse it. It manages connection pooling and multiplexing for you. Always set timeouts to prevent your app from hanging.

beats.title: Async Requests
beats.narration: Send async requests to keep your threads free. It returns a CompletableFuture, allowing you to chain operations as the data arrives.

beats.title: Streaming Large Files
beats.subtitle: Avoid heap memory issues

nodes.label: BodyPublishers
nodes.detail: Stream file from disk to socket

nodes.label: BodyHandlers
nodes.detail: Stream socket to file on disk

beats.narration: For large files, don't load them into memory. Use BodyPublishers and BodyHandlers to stream data directly between disk and the network socket.
